name: Kozhikkodan (Calicut) halwa tradition
tagline: SM Street's jewel‑toned halwas and artisanal makers draw renewed visitor interest
summary: Kozhikkodan halwa — the coconut‑oil halwa of Calicut — anchors sweets trails on SM Street, where family bakeries and artisanal makers sell colourful, long‑lasting halwa as souvenirs.
description: Kozhikkodan halwa (often called Calicut halwa) is a dense, glossy sweet made traditionally with wheat/starch, sugar or jaggery, coconut oil and often eggs and nuts. Its distinctive texture and long shelf life make it a popular souvenir and street‑food attraction in Kozhikode.

SM Street (Mittayi Theruvu or 'Sweet Meat Street') is the urban heart of the tradition — a row of long‑running bakeries and halwa makers where halwa is cooked and displayed in jewel tones. The halwa tradition ties to the city’s trading history and to immigrant sweetmakers who helped shape local confectionery styles.

In recent years halwa shops and small artisanal makers feature on food walks, local life‑experience trails and travel guides, bringing renewed attention from domestic and foreign visitors as Kozhikode grows as a food‑tourism stop.

Producers face commercial pressure (for example fluctuations in coconut‑oil prices), and some makers adapt with new flavours, small‑pack retail and online sales. Visitors who follow a halwa or sweets trail get a mix of historic shops, live cooking views and modern artisanal labels reviving older recipes.
highlights: SM Street (Mittayi Theruvu) — traditional halwa shops and bakeries
Distinctive coconut‑oil halwa (wheat/starch base; fruit, nut and banana varieties)
Food / sweets trails and life‑experience walking tours that include halwa
Generational family shops alongside new artisanal brands and startups
Halwa as a durable, packable souvenir for travellers

sections.heading: Background
body: Kozhikkodan halwa becomes part of Kozhikode’s identity through street commerce and bakery culture. European traders once called the local sweet ‘sweetmeat’, and a thoroughfare known as Sweet Meat Street (S.M. Street or Mittayi Theruvu) preserves that name and the concentration of halwa shops.

The local style uses coconut oil (not ghee) and a starch or wheat base; makers produce many varieties — plain wheat halwa, banana halwa, fruit and nut halwas — and sellers keep halwa in stacked glass cases so visitors can choose by colour and texture.

sections.heading: What to see and do
body: Walk Mittayi Theruvu to see halwa displayed in cubes and tubs, watch small production stations or family kitchens at work, and sample several varieties. Food writers and local guides include halwa stops on Kozhikode food trails and walking tours.
Combine halwa sampling with nearby market experiences (spices, banana chips, bakeries). Look for legacy names alongside newer artisanal labels that package halwa for shipping and online sales.

sections.heading: Plan your visit
body: Halwa shops are open year‑round; mornings and early evenings are lively times on SM Street. Kozhikode’s tourism season (cooler months) runs roughly October–March when city walks are most comfortable.

Buy halwa in sealed packs for travel, ask about ingredients if you have allergies (many varieties contain egg or nuts), and confirm freshness when purchasing larger quantities. If you want a behind‑the‑scenes look, check Kerala Tourism life‑experience trails or local guides that include halwa makers on their itineraries.

visitorInfo.bestTime: October–March (cooler months; food walks are more comfortable)
visitorInfo.howToReach: Kozhikode is served by Calicut International Airport (Karipur), Kozhikode Railway Station and regular bus services; SM Street lies in central Kozhikode and is walkable from the city centre — confirm local connections before travel.
etiquette: Buy small sealed packets first to test flavours and for easier packing.
Ask about ingredients (eggs, nuts, ghee) if you have allergies.
Visit early evening or mid‑morning to see halwa being packed and to avoid peak crowds.
Ask shopkeepers before photographing inside production areas or kitchens.
